content: Female ejaculation, also referred to as squirting or gushing, is the release of a noticeable amount of clear fluid from the paraurethral ducts and/or urethra in human females during orgasm. The precise origin of this fluid remains a topic of debate, though some researchers suggest it is produced by the Skene's glands, which are often considered the female equivalent of the prostate. For much of the 20th century, the existence of female ejaculation was controversial, and it was often confused with urinary incontinence. However, scientific studies conducted since the 1980s have confirmed that female ejaculation is a distinct phenomenon unrelated to urination. Female ejaculation is commonly associated with stimulation of the urethral sponge, an area sometimes referred to as the G-spot, located near the anterior vaginal wall. In some cases, ejaculation can also occur through external stimulation of the clitoris, as the internal clitoral tissue contracts and stimulates the urethral tissue. The phenomenon of female ejaculation has been documented in medical, anatomical, and biological literature since ancient times. Aristotle, the Greek philosopher, mentioned it, and Galen, a Roman physician in the 2nd century, described the female prostate. During the Italian Renaissance, anatomist Renaldus Columbus discussed female ejaculate in relation to the clitoris. In the 17th century, Dutch anatomist Regnier de Graaf wrote extensively about female anatomy and described the release of fluid during sexual arousal. Despite its historical documentation, female ejaculation was largely ignored by the medical community until the 1980s, when the book The G-Spot by Ladas, Whipple, and Perry brought attention to the topic. This book not only validated the existence of the G-spot but also highlighted female ejaculation as an important aspect of women's sexual health. Although the medical and scientific communities now acknowledge the existence of female ejaculation, there is still a lack of comprehensive scientific understanding regarding the mechanisms of ejaculation and the exact source of the fluid. Research has shown that the fluid is not urine but rather an alkaline liquid secreted by the paraurethral glands. These glands produce prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) and prostate-specific antigen (PSA), both of which are also produced by the male prostate. Additionally, the Skene's glands produce Human Protein 1, a protein once thought to be unique to the male prostate. Studies indicate that 54-60% of women have experienced fluid emission during orgasm, with 6% reporting regular, forceful ejaculation and 13% experiencing it infrequently. Dr. Gary Schubach has suggested that the majority of women are capable of ejaculation, even if they are unaware of it. Female ejaculation has also been referenced in ancient Indian and Chinese texts. In Sanskrit, the fluid is called Amrita, meaning divine nectar, and it was believed to have medicinal properties. The esoteric Buddhist practice of Tantra placed particular emphasis on this phenomenon in its sexual rituals. Chemical analyses of the fluid have revealed the presence of glucose and fructose, which are natural sugars also found in male prostatic fluid. The fluid also contains PSA, a protein produced by the prostate gland in males and believed to be secreted by the Skene's glands in females. While the fluid may contain trace amounts of creatinine and urea, which are markers of urine, these levels are significantly lower than those found in urine samples. In 1988, Dr. Milan Zaviacic conducted a study on five women and found that the fluid contained higher concentrations of fructose than urine. In 1997, Dr. F. Cabello Santamaria analyzed post-orgasmic urine samples and found PSA concentrations in 75% of cases, which were absent in pre-orgasmic samples. Fluid collected at the point of orgasm consistently showed the presence of PSA. In 2002, Dr. Emanuele Jannini suggested that the variability in the size of Skene's gland openings, which can be as small as pinholes or appear absent in some women, might explain why not all women experience visible ejaculation. The Skene's glands, also known as the female prostate or paraurethral glands, are homologous to the male prostate. These glands develop from the same embryonic tissue as the male prostate and are located near the urethra. The size and structure of these glands vary significantly among women. During sexual arousal, the glands fill with fluid, which may be expelled into the urethra or, in some cases, into the vagina. The swelling of the paraurethral tissue during arousal is due to both the filling of the glands and the engorgement of erectile tissue, such as the corpus cavernosum clitoridis, which is homologous to the erectile tissue in the male penis. The rhythmic contractions of pelvic muscles during orgasm are believed to expel the accumulated fluid, resulting in female ejaculation. The volume of fluid released can vary widely, ranging from a small amount to as much as one to one and a half liters in some cases, as observed in in vivo studies. Misinformation about female ejaculation can lead to misdiagnoses of medical conditions. For example, some women may mistake female ejaculation for urinary incontinence and seek unnecessary medical treatments, such as surgery or medications. Additionally, the expulsion of large amounts of fluid from the vagina, which is distinct from female ejaculation, may indicate conditions such as infections, sexually transmitted diseases, or physiological discharge. It is important for women experiencing abnormal vaginal discharge to undergo a medical evaluation to rule out underlying conditions. In the United Kingdom, the British Board of Film Classification (BBFC) has not officially recognized female ejaculation, claiming that all instances they have reviewed in media appear to be urination during sexual activity. As a result, depictions of female ejaculation remain absent from UK-classified adult films.
